title: No title – About the sea

paragraphs.text: People find the sea both inspiring and calming. It is in constant motion but never seems to change. The whisper of rising tide over sand is the same today as it was when 17th-century navigators rocked at anchor in a Caribbean bay. The radiant blue of the Mediterranean dazzles in the same way as it did when Hannibal* set forth with his fleet to conquer Rome, over two thousand years ago. But many of the marine creatures that played in the waves around their ships are rare today, already in deep trouble and needing our help.

The first commercial fishermen cast their nets and hooks over a thousand years ago. Fisheries intensified over the centuries, but even in the 19th century it was still felt, justifiably, that the plentiful resources of the sea were, for the most part, beyond the reach of fishing, and so there was little need to restrict fishing or create protected areas. However, the 20th century heralded an escalation in fishing that was unprecedented in the history of the oceans, and modern fishing technologies now leave fish with no place to hide. Today, the only refuges from fishing are those that we deliberately create. Unhappily, the sea trails far behind the land in terms of area and quality of protection given.

For centuries we have held onto the notion that the sea is not the same as the land. We still view the sea as a place where people and nations should be free to come and go at will, as well as somewhere that we should be free to exploit. On land, protected areas have proliferated in response to a rise in the number of people on the planet. Here, we have made greater headway in maintaining the richness and variety of wildlife and landscape. Currently, 12 per cent of the world’s land is within protected areas, compared to under 1 per cent for the sea. Worse still, most marine protected areas allow fishing to continue. Areas off-limits to all exploitation cover something like one five-thousandth of the total area of the world’s seas. We have to be bold and move rapidly if we are to do something about this.

A starting gun has already been fired. In 2000, the US president issued an executive order, endorsed by subsequent administrations, charging government agencies to create a national network of marine protected areas. At the World Summit on Sustainable Development in 2002, coastal nations of the world pledged to create national networks of marine protected areas within a decade. Meanwhile, European nations had already committed to the creation of a Europe-wide network. However, these pledges were vague on targets for numbers or size of protected areas, and how they should be managed.

Several countries have made good progress. South Africa undertook to protect 20 per cent of its waters. Already 18 per cent of its territorial waters are reserves and the network is being expanded offshore. In Australia, a third of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park was protected from fishing in 2004. The protected areas in this network were chosen because they are representative of all the different habitats in the park, and the initiative set a shining example for others to follow. Britain's Royal Commission on Environmental Pollution recommended in 2004 that 30 per cent of the country’s waters should become marine reserves. We are on the path to a global network of marine reserves, where fishing is completely prohibited, that could restore the oceans to much of their former glory.

Can the world afford to protect the oceans? One estimate, made in 2004, put the cost at around £8 billion per year to run a worldwide network of marine reserves covering 30 per cent of all oceans and seas. Initial one-time set-up costs would be about five times this amount. These sums seem considerable, but are put in perspective when we consider that they are less than the £8.8 to £17.6 billion we currently spend on harmful subsidies that encourage excess fishing capacity. Most countries offer fishermen tax breaks on fuel, for example, or free nets, and many countries pay for access to fish in another country’s waters. Compared to global defence spending, estimated at £530 billion in 2004, the sums needed to keep our oceans healthy are trivial. The costs are also less than the £18.2 billion that Europeans and North Americans collectively spend on ice cream, and roughly equate to the £8.8 billion we spend on perfumes, or £8.2 billion on ocean cruises.

In addition, a worldwide reserve network would create more than a million permanent jobs for managers, wardens and administrators. Much of the running costs of coastal reserves could be recouped from visitors. Some, like the Saba and Bonaire marine parks in the Caribbean are already self-funding, based on modest payments made by visitors. The world can certainly afford marine reserves. What it cannot afford is to be without them.
